analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit their supply chains for forced labor and report the results to the government.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2020 with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate labor committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any publicly traded company with more than $500 million in annual worldwide revenue to audit its supply chains every year for forced labor and human trafficking, and to investigate its direct suppliers, secondary suppliers, and on-site service providers like cafeteria and cleaning contractors. Companies would have to file the results with the Department of Labor, publish them on their websites, and have their chief executive sign a sworn certification that the findings are complete. The Labor Department could fine violators up to $100 million, and up to $500 million more for willful violations, and would report violators to Congress each year.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be workers trapped in forced labor at home and abroad, who would gain a powerful new check: independent auditors interviewing them off-site, with pay stubs cross-checked against employer records and anti-retaliation protections written into supplier contracts. Consumers would gain a searchable annual disclosure of where forced labor appears in the products and services they buy. Honest companies that already police their supply chains would gain a level playing field against competitors that profit from unpaid labor.

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual audits covering direct suppliers, secondary suppliers, and on-site service providers, with auditors required to interview a cross-section of workers — on-site and off-site, including minors with age-sensitive techniques — and collect pay stubs to compare against employer records [S3].
Requires companies to publish the audit report on their websites with a link on the homepage, so consumers can see what forced labor was found in their supply chains [S3].

Requires the CEO to sign a sworn certification that the company exercised due diligence and disclosed every known instance of forced labor, with criminal liability for false statements under the federal False Statements Act [S3].
Bars suppliers from retaliating against workers who participate in the audits, and protects audit participation through normal workplace grievance procedures [S3].

Gives the Labor Department authority to assess civil damages up to $100 million, punitive damages up to $500 million for willful violations, and to seek court injunctions where violations endanger workers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on large publicly traded companies, which would pay for annual third-party audits of their entire supply chains and face fines reaching into the hundreds of millions of dollars. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers in higher prices, and companies that fail would face public exposure of forced labor in their supply chains.

drawbacks.text: Annual audits of a full supply chain — direct suppliers, secondary suppliers, and on-site contractors — would be expensive for large companies, and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers in higher prices [S3].

The law relies heavily on company self-reporting: the company chooses its auditors, writes the report, and files it with a CEO certification, so a company determined to conceal forced labor could produce clean-looking reports unless regulators catch discrepancies — the bill provides no independent agency auditors and no automated verification [S3].
The $500 million revenue threshold exempts every smaller company, so forced labor in the supply chains of businesses below that size would go entirely unexamined [S3].

A good-faith objection from business: layered on top of existing state disclosure laws and customs-enforcement bans on forced-labor imports, this adds another annual reporting regime whose real-world effect on actual labor conditions, as opposed to paperwork, is unproven [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but indirect: this is a transparency-and-pressure bill, not a direct rescue program. Its teeth — off-site worker interviews, pay-stub verification, CEO sworn certifications, and fines up to $600 million — are stronger than typical corporate disclosure laws, and anti-retaliation protections address the main reason audits miss abuse. The weaknesses are that enforcement depends on the company's own reports and regulators reading them, that the largest violation exposed in a report may be remediated on paper, and that companies under the revenue threshold escape entirely. On balance it would meaningfully raise the cost of using forced labor without materially restricting anyone's freedom.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on July 21, 2020 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House consideration before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multinational companies and their shareholders benefit from what actually happened: they avoid mandatory annual forced-labor audits, public disclosure of their supply chains, sworn CEO certifications, and potential fines up to $600 million. Companies already running third-party audits voluntarily also avoid a compliance burden that would have applied to competitors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large multinationals that escaped new audits

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so party positions can only be inferred from the fact that a Republican sponsor attracted no cosponsors from either party before the bill died in committee [S4].

industries.industry: Large multinational corporations (retail, apparel, electronics, food, tech — any issuer over $500M revenue)
industries.note: They would bear annual third-party audit costs across their full supply chains, publish what auditors find on their websites, have CEOs sign sworn certifications, and face civil fines up to $100 million and punitive fines up to $500 million. Companies profiting from cheap forced labor would lose the advantage; costs of compliance would partly flow to consumers.

industries.industry: Third-party labor audit and compliance firms
industries.note: The bill creates a guaranteed annual market for supply-chain audits by thousands of companies. Independent auditors also gain formal standing to interview workers confidentially and off-site, which could surface real abuses.
